column5: Rab as flock-owner and shepherd
column6: The psalm names YHWH as the speaker's shepherd, giving the source's Rab who owns and directs the herd a direct divine pastoral frame.

column5: green pastures and resting waters
column6: The shepherd brings the dependent flock to nourishing pasture and rest, closely matching the commentary's owner who brings the herd to a protected grazing place.

column5: restore and guide in right paths
column6: The same shepherd restores and leads the person on paths; this makes the source's هدى B003 front-leading image part of pastoral care rather than mere travel.

column5: we are his; people and sheep of his pasture
column6: The verse joins belonging to the creator with being the sheep of his pasture, directly combining the source's Rab-as-owner with its herd and grazing scene.

column5: cattle on a thousand hills are mine
column6: God's claim over cattle supplies a concrete biblical form for the commentary's insistence that Rab is the owner before he is the herd's guide.

column5: ox knows owner; donkey its master's manger
column6: Isaiah makes an animal's recognition of its owner and feeding-place a rebuke to Israel; it adds a reversal to the source's animal scene and its later naming of one's own Rab.

column5: green vegetation assigned as animal food
column6: The creation decree gives green plants to land animals for food, a direct scriptural counterpart to God bringing forth pasture for livestock.

column5: grass for livestock and food for people
column6: The land blessing explicitly moves from grass supplied for cattle to human eating, paralleling the commentary's pasture as provision for both people and their animals.

column5: grass for cattle; plants and food for humans
column6: The psalm treats the sprouting of grass for cattle and human food as God's work, closely matching the source's creator of pasture and its 79:33 and 80:31 provision motif.

column5: rain makes grass grow on mountains
column6: God covers the sky, prepares rain, and sprouts grass on the mountains; this connects divine production of grazing land with the commentary's mountain-and-pasture association.

column5: God gives food to beasts
column6: The creator's provision of food to animals makes explicit the care for livestock that the source reads into pasture.

column5: leader goes before the people; sheep without shepherd
column6: Moses asks for a successor who goes out before and brings in the congregation so it is not sheep without a shepherd; it directly joins the source's Musa setting, B003 leading-from-the-front, and ruler-as-shepherd.

column5: Moses and Aaron lead God's people like a flock
column6: The psalm says God led the people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, giving the commentary's Moses-linked scene a divine owner, human agents, and flock in one verse.

column5: ruler commissioned to shepherd Israel
column6: Israel tells David that he will shepherd God's people and be their ruler; its royal formula is a precise analogue to the source's B002 equation of governor and shepherd.

column5: God leads people as sheep and guides them as flock
column6: The wilderness exodus is described with both flock-leading and guidance, closely matching the source's single work of owner, guide, and herd.

column5: David shepherds with integrity and skillful guidance
column6: David's shepherding is defined by inner integrity and skilled leading, developing the source's claim that pastoral language can describe competent public rule.

column5: gather, carry, and gently lead the flock
column6: The divine shepherd gathers vulnerable lambs, carries them, and gently leads nursing ewes; it gives concrete protective actions to the source's guarded pasture and leading owner.

column5: God gathers and keeps Israel as a shepherd
column6: The one who scattered Israel gathers and guards it as a shepherd guards a flock, making protection and restoration integral to divine ownership.

column5: shepherd-rulers feed themselves instead of flock
column6: Ezekiel's indictment turns the source's ruler-as-shepherd image into a negative test: leaders who consume provision themselves fail the flock entrusted to them.

column5: God gathers sheep and feeds them on mountains
column6: God himself brings the scattered flock out, gathers it, and feeds it on the mountains; this is a particularly close scene of owner, leading, and pasture.

column5: good pasture and secure grazing land
column6: The promised sheep receive good pasture and lie down in rich grazing land, supplying the protected-pasture element of the source without reducing it to a word match.

column5: source ر ع ي B002/B003/B007; Hebrew רעה and מרעה
column6: The Hebrew verb for tending and noun for pasture are cognate with the source's ر ع ي family; here they describe God feeding sheep in a good pasture, including both the source's shepherd and marʿā senses.

column5: God himself pastures and gives rest
column6: The divine speaker personally shepherds the flock and makes it lie down, the clearest biblical formulation of the commentary's owner who both leads and supplies the grazing place.

column5: David appointed as one shepherd
column6: God appoints David as the flock's shepherd, preserving the distinction between the ultimate owner and a commissioned human ruler developed in the source.

column5: pasture on every bare height
column6: In the restoration promise, the released people feed along the ways and find pasture even on bare heights; it extends the source's pasture image into guided return and unexpected provision.

column5: guide to springs after hunger and thirst
column6: The compassionate leader guides the redeemed to water after removing hunger and thirst, pairing direction with provision as the commentary does.

column5: ruler stands and shepherds in the LORD's strength
column6: Micah joins rule, secure dwelling, and shepherding in the strength of God, a direct royal form of the source's ruler who tends his people.

column5: source ر ع ي B002/B007; Hebrew רְעוּ pasture the flock
column6: Jacob's well scene tells the herdsmen to water the flock and then go pasture it; the Hebrew cognate shows the source's ر ع ي family in an ordinary husbandry setting.

column5: grass withers when the LORD's breath blows
column6: The grass fades under God's breath, furnishing a close biblical image for the source's pasture that is later made into dark debris and for its turn toward the temporary world.

column5: grass fades but God's word endures
column6: The contrast between fading grass and what endures gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's move from temporary worldly provision to the better, lasting life.

column5: Moses carries the thirsty straying lamb
column6: The midrash makes Moses's compassionate attention to a runaway lamb the reason God entrusts Israel to him; it turns the source's Musa-and-shepherd scene into a criterion for protective leadership.

column5: leader must go out and come in before Israel
column6: The exposition of Numbers 27:17 reads Moses's request as one for a leader present with the people rather than distant from them, sharpening the source's image of the animal that leads the others from in front.

column5: source ر ع ي B002; Aramaic rʿyā for shepherd
column6: The Aramaic witness retains the congregation-as-sheep-without-a-shepherd image in Moses's succession request; its rʿyā is a cognate of the source's rāʿī and still carries public leadership.

column5: calls own sheep and leads them out
column6: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, an unusually exact New Testament counterpart to the source's owner and B003 animal-leader scene.

column5: goes before sheep and they follow
column6: The shepherd goes ahead of the sheep and they follow his known voice, directly realizing the commentary's detail of front animals guiding those behind.

column5: go in and out and find pasture
column6: Within the shepherd discourse, entering through Jesus leads to safety and pasture; it joins protection with access to grazing as in the source's unified scene.

column5: good shepherd lays down life for sheep
column6: The good shepherd's self-giving makes protection of the flock more radical than the source's lexical description of the shepherd who surrounds and preserves livestock.

column5: hired hand does not own sheep and abandons them
column6: The contrast hinges on ownership and guarding: a hireling flees while the true shepherd's sheep are endangered, a negative foil to the source's owner who protects the herd.

column5: shepherd knows his own sheep
column6: Mutual recognition between shepherd and sheep develops the source's closing move in which the person names this owner as his own Rab.

column5: ruler who will shepherd Israel
column6: Matthew's citation calls the coming figure both ruler and shepherd of Israel, precisely echoing the source's ruler/shepherd equation.

column5: crowd as sheep without shepherd; Jesus teaches
column6: Jesus responds to a shepherdless crowd by teaching it, making guidance of people the action expected from the missing shepherd.

column5: commission to shepherd my sheep
column6: The risen Jesus entrusts his own sheep to Peter's care, distinguishing the flock's owner from the human leader who is commissioned to tend it.

column5: overseers shepherd God's acquired flock
column6: The elders must watch over the whole flock and shepherd God's assembly; it makes pastoral rule explicitly attentive and accountable, resonating with B002 and the source's B003 watchfulness.

column5: return to shepherd and overseer of souls
column6: Straying sheep return to a shepherd who is also an overseer, joining restoration, guidance, and supervisory care in the source's pastoral image.

column5: elders shepherd God's flock with oversight
column6: The elders' charge makes shepherding a form of responsible oversight, giving a Christian communal application to the source's ruler who tends a people.

column5: chief shepherd appears
column6: The title chief shepherd places local shepherd-leaders under a higher shepherd, akin to the source's distinction between the owner and those who lead within the herd scene.

column5: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of life
column6: The Lamb becomes the shepherd who guides the flock to living-water springs; it carries the source's pasture-and-guidance image into its own enduring, eschatological setting.

column5: ruling nations expressed by the shepherd verb
column6: The royal judge's rule over nations is stated with the verb to shepherd, preserving the political sense of tending subjects foregrounded in source B002.

column5: all flesh like grass; grass withers
column6: Peter applies fading grass to human mortality, a direct Christian extension of the source's pasture-to-debris and worldly-transience turn.

column5: word remains forever
column6: The verse's enduring word completes the preceding grass image with a lasting contrast, comparable to the source's contrast between worldly life and what remains.

column5: source ر ع ي B002; Syriac rʿyā, shepherd
column6: The Peshitta's Syriac rʿyā for Jesus as the good shepherd is cognate with Arabic rāʿī in the source and uses the shared root for self-giving flock care.

column5: Moses pastures Jethro's flock to Horeb
column6: The biblical Moses first appears at Horeb while tending and leading a flock; alongside the commentary's explicit Musa setting, this gives a concrete narrative pastoral setting without claiming the two accounts are the same scene.

column5: Moses protects shepherds and waters their flock
column6: Moses drives away attackers and waters the flock for Midianite shepherds, a specific earlier portrayal of the protective action the source assigns to a shepherd.

column5: land belongs to God; people are temporary residents
column6: God's ownership of land and the people's temporary tenancy give a land-based counterpart to the source's Rab-as-owner and its explanation of pasture as temporary metāʿ.

column5: Lord of sheep and accountable appointed shepherds
column6: The Animal Apocalypse represents Israel as sheep under the Lord of the sheep and appointed shepherds whose stewardship is judged; it expands the source's owner, flock, and delegated leaders into an apocalyptic history.

column5: owner seeks the one lost sheep
column6: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the lost sheep, making the source's enclosing and preserving shepherd an active seeker rather than only a keeper of pasture.

column5: Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep
column6: The title great shepherd binds communal pastoral imagery to the God of peace and resurrection, a Christian theological development of the source's divine owner/shepherd.

column5: grass today, cast into an oven tomorrow
column6: Jesus uses grass's brief life to teach trust in God's provision; the image closely meets the source's created pasture that soon changes, while its argument concerns anxious humans rather than livestock.

column4: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 46
column5: Christ as good shepherd versus hireling
column6: Augustine's exposition of John 10 reads the good shepherd's care and self-giving as Christological, giving a major Christian interpretive frame for the owner, flock, and protective contrast in the source.

column5: angel of repentance appears as shepherd
column6: Hermas receives moral commands from a shepherd figure; this later Christian use turns pastoral guidance into corrective formation, a plausible extension of the source's Rab-as-corrector within its herd image.

column5: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
column6: The verse makes Israel both God's people and the sheep held in his hand; its call to hear his voice joins ownership, pastoral care, and responsive recognition of the Rab.

column5: Shepherd of Israel leads Joseph like a flock
column6: The invocation directly addresses God as Israel's shepherd and asks him to lead Joseph as a flock, concentrating the source's owner and front-leading functions.

column5: shepherd and carry God's inheritance forever
column6: The plea asks God to save, bless, shepherd, and carry his people forever; it makes protective pastoral rule explicitly enduring, relevant to the source's turn from temporary pasture to what lasts.

column5: God has shepherded Jacob all his life
column6: Jacob calls God the one who has been his shepherd throughout life, giving the source's personal naming of one's Rab a concentrated ancestral precedent.

column5: flock of God's pasture gives thanks forever
column6: The flock-of-your-pasture formula culminates in perpetual thanksgiving; it brings the source's opening glorification of the Rab into the pastoral relation itself.

column5: David taken from pasture and following sheep to rule Israel
column6: God recalls taking David from following sheep to be prince over Israel, making the shepherd-to-ruler transition explicit rather than merely metaphorical.

column5: David pursues a predator and rescues the lamb
column6: David's shepherding includes going after the lion or bear and delivering the sheep from its mouth, a concrete protective action for the source's keeper who guards livestock.

column5: shepherd bears loss for animals torn or stolen
column6: Jacob describes accepting liability for flock losses rather than passing them to the owner; this gives a demanding economic form to the source's protective shepherd.

column5: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
column6: The instruction requires sustained, informed attention to a herd, closely matching the source's B003 extension from shepherding to watching where a matter is going.

column5: old grass passes and new growth appears
column6: The pastoral maxim traces hay's disappearance, fresh growth, and mountain vegetation; it offers a close agrarian counterpart to pasture brought forth and then transformed.

column5: rain, abundant bread, and livestock grazing broad pasture
column6: The promised divine rain produces abundance and broad pasture for cattle, directly matching the commentary's creator who produces grazing provision for people and animals.

column5: working oxen and donkeys eat prepared fodder
column6: Farm animals receive rich fodder while doing agricultural work, a close counterpart to the source's B007 detail of working animals grazing around a settled community.

column5: Moses gives water to congregation and livestock
column6: God instructs Moses to bring water from the rock for both the people and their animals; it is a specific Mosaic scene of shared human-and-livestock provision.

column5: just rule in the fear of God
column6: David's oracle defines the God-fearing ruler whose effect is developed in the next verse; it supplies the governing member of the source's shepherd-ruler image.

column5: rain causes grass to sprout from the earth
column6: The next line compares the just ruler's advent to light and rain that sprouts grass, a striking joining of righteous rule with the growth of the source's pasture.

column5: pastures clothed with flocks and fields sing
column6: Pastures are filled with flocks and the fertile landscape shouts and sings; it lets the source's opening praise encompass the very pasture and herd that God causes to thrive.

column5: evil-doers sprout like grass only for destruction
column6: The psalm uses flourishing grass for a short-lived prosperity that ends in destruction, closely paralleling the source's pasture that becomes debris and its warning about transient life.

column5: the Most High is forever
column6: The contrast calls YHWH the Most High forever, joining the source's al-Aʿlā title to its contrast between fading grass and enduring reality.

column5: wise instruction given by one shepherd
column6: Ecclesiastes attributes wisdom that prods and steadies its hearers to one shepherd, extending the source's pastoral guide into correction and instruction.

column5: failed shepherds do not strengthen, heal, bind, seek, or restore
column6: The detailed catalogue says what pastoral rule owes the vulnerable flock; it concretizes the source's claim that the shepherd surrounds and preserves those in his care.

column5: God seeks lost, restores strayed, binds injured, and strengthens weak
column6: God's own response reverses failed leadership through specific acts of search, restoration, and healing, deepening the source's owner-protector scene.

column5: human sheep of God's pasture
column6: The chapter's conclusion explicitly calls the people God's sheep and flock of his pasture, completing the source's owner, people, and grazing-place relation.

column5: shepherds after God's heart feed knowledge and understanding
column6: God promises leaders who feed the people with knowledge and discernment, making pastoral governance an intellectual and moral guidance like the source's leading function.

column5: shepherds lead sheep astray from their resting place
column6: The lost sheep are misdirected by their shepherds through the mountains and forget their resting place; this is a pointed negative reversal of the source's guide who brings a flock to pasture.

column5: shepherd rescues remnants from a lion's mouth
column6: Amos's image of a shepherd recovering only a leg or ear from a predator gives a grim, concrete limit case for the source's protecting shepherd.

column5: foolish shepherd neither seeks, heals, nor nourishes
column6: The false shepherd neglects the lost and injured and consumes the fat flock instead; this negative portrait tests every protective and provisioning element developed in the source.

column5: grazing leads to fullness, pride, and forgetting the owner
column6: Hosea depicts pasture and fullness producing self-exaltation and forgetfulness of God, an ethical counterpoint to the source's pasture as temporary provision under its owner.

column5: Davidic king shepherds the Lord's flock faithfully
column6: The psalm portrays the hoped-for Davidic ruler as faithfully shepherding the Lord's flock, preventing their stumbling in pasture and leading them in holiness; it fuses delegated rule, divine ownership, and guidance.

column5: eternal life and no snatching from the shepherd's hand
column6: Jesus gives the sheep unending life and guarantees that no one will snatch them away, bringing the source's guarded flock and its lasting-life contrast together.

column5: fierce wolves will not spare the flock
column6: Paul's warning supplies the threat that makes pastoral watchfulness necessary, sharpening the source's protective shepherd rather than repeating its generic title.

column5: leaders do not dominate but become examples to the flock
column6: The elders are forbidden to lord it over those entrusted to them and instead model conduct; it qualifies the source's ruler-shepherd relation with a specific non-dominating form of leadership.

column5: flock no longer hungers or thirsts
column6: The eschatological community's freedom from hunger and thirst supplies the provision that the following shepherd-and-springs image brings to completion, echoing the source's pasture and lasting-life movement.

column5: pastors joined with teachers in communal leadership
column6: The risen Christ gives pastors-and-teachers to the community, a concise Christian institutional use of shepherd language for guiding and forming people.

column5: Paul rereads the unmuzzled ox command for apostolic support
column6: Paul cites the Torah's feeding of a working ox and asks how its principle bears on apostolic workers; this is a deliberate interpretive reapplication of animal provision, not simply a duplicate pasture image.

column5: the world passes away while the doer of God's will remains
column6: The verse gives a direct Christian formulation of the source's distinction between the passing worldly life reached through temporary provision and what endures.

column5: riches and crown do not endure
column6: Following the flock-watch instruction, the proverb states that wealth and political standing are not permanent; its own transience claim clarifies why the source calls pasture provision temporary metāʿ.

column5: working ox must not be muzzled
column6: The law protects an animal's access to food while it works, a concrete ethical analogue to the source's working camels and livestock sustained by grazing.

column5: camels receive straw and fodder at a household
column6: The servant's camels are unloaded and supplied with straw and fodder at the house, a specific narrative counterpart to the source's camels grazing around people and dwellings.

column5: God makes grass sprout in desolate ground
column6: God satisfies wasteland and makes grass grow where people do not cultivate it; this extends the source's pasture-maker to nonhuman and wild terrain.

column5: God declares the end from the beginning
column6: The source explicitly makes the pasture's maker one who sees what it will become; Isaiah's divine knowledge of end from beginning is a precise theological bridge for that secondary claim.

column5: a child leads reconciled wild and domestic animals
column6: The future peace scene gives a child the action of leading a mixed animal company, an indirect but specific counterpart to the source's B003 image of a leader before other animals.

column5: cow and bear graze; lion eats straw like ox
column6: The transformed creation is pictured through shared grazing and fodder among animals, a distinct eschatological extension of the source's pasture and livestock scene.

column5: the righteous knows an animal's needs
column6: The proverb makes attentive care for an animal a mark of righteousness, giving an ethical consequence to the source's shepherd who protects livestock.

column5: one who tends a flock shares its milk
column6: Paul's pastoral labor analogy assumes that the flock's keeper receives its produce, linking the source's pasture as provision with the work of tending it.

column5: plowman and thresher work in hope of a share
column6: Paul states the human-worker application of the ox text: laborers should expect a share of the yield. It reframes the source's livestock provision as a principle about those who serve a community.

column5: little flock and the Father's gift of the kingdom
column6: Jesus calls the disciples a little flock while locating their security in the Father's gift of the kingdom, joining pastoral belonging with the source's movement beyond temporary worldly provision.

column5: seen things are temporary and unseen things eternal
column6: Paul's temporal-eternal contrast is a close Christian formulation of the source's conclusion about the worldly life and the more enduring reality, though it does not itself use pasture imagery.

column5: shepherd separates sheep from goats at judgment
column6: The final judgment is pictured through a shepherd sorting a mixed herd; it gives the source's animal scene an eschatological use distinct from provisioning and protection.

column5: struck shepherd and scattered sheep
column6: The passion prediction reverses the source's secure owner-and-flock scene: when the shepherd is struck, the sheep scatter, showing the flock's dependence on its guide.

column5: lost largest sheep sought over the ninety-nine
column6: This Christian apocryphal version makes the wandering sheep the largest and specially loved one; it is a distinctive reception of the owner who actively seeks and values a member of the flock.
